title: Implement Magic Dictionary
prompt:
A magic dictionary is built from a list of distinct words. It supports a `search(query)` operation that returns `true` if changing exactly one character of `query` (to a different character, not to itself) produces a word that exists in the dictionary. It returns `false` otherwise — in particular, the query itself matching a dictionary word with zero changes does not count.

Implement `magic_dictionary_search(dictionary, queries)`: build the dictionary from `dictionary` up front, then return a list of booleans, one per entry in `queries`, indicating the search result for each.

examples.explanation: "hello" needs 0 changes to match itself, so it doesn't count. "hhllo" becomes "hello" with exactly one change. "hell" has different length from any word. "leetcoded" also has no length match.
"a" matches itself with 0 changes (doesn't count) and can't reach "ab" (different length). "b" becomes "a" with exactly one change.
With a single-character dictionary word, "a" matches itself with zero changes (doesn't count), while "b" becomes "a" with exactly one change, the smallest possible query length.

constraints: dictionary[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
All strings in dictionary are distinct
queries[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing a query against every dictionary word of the same length directly works (and is fine given the small constraints), but a trie lets you prune shared prefixes and generalizes better.

Insert all dictionary words into a trie. Then do a DFS over the query alongside the trie, and allow exactly one position where you branch into a child whose character differs from the query's character at that spot.
Track whether you've already 'used up' your one allowed mismatch as you recurse; a match only counts if you land on an end-of-word node having used the mismatch exactly once, not zero times.

solution.approach: Build a trie from the dictionary words. To search a query, run a recursive DFS that walks the query alongside the trie while tracking how many mismatches have been used (0 or 1). At each position, if a child matches the query's character, recurse with the mismatch budget unchanged; additionally, if the budget still allows it (no mismatch used yet), recurse into every other child as a 'used a mismatch' branch. A search succeeds if any path reaches the end of the query at a word-end node having used exactly one mismatch — zero mismatches used means it's an exact match, which doesn't count.
solution.timeComplexity: O(sum of dictionary word lengths) to build, O(26 * L) per query in the worst case
